articles.description:
Every byte matters when optimizing web performance, but not every project has a build pipeline to strip unnecessary whitespace and developer comments from HTML. You might be staring at a bloated markup file from a legacy CMS or an exported prototype, needing to shave kilobytes off its size without installing a single dependency. The HTML Minifier on DevTools solves this friction point by offering an instant, browser-based minification engine that respects your code’s logic while slimming its payload.
The HTML Minifier is a client-side tool that compresses HTML documents by removing characters browsers ignore: extraneous spaces, line breaks, indentation, and HTML comments. The page’s visual output remains unchanged. Because the entire process runs in your local browser, no code ever leaves …
articles.title: HTML Minifier: the privacy-first data tool that runs entirely in your browser

The next thing will ship with the same defect in a fresh costume.
Someone replied: "See you when it does."
It took two days. And the thing I got wrong wasn't the timing. It was that I spent those two days watching the wrong room.

When it turned out nothing was checking whether the drill still ran, I put a separate machine on a separate schedule to watch for its proof of life.
All of it aimed at one thing: my code.
So when I said the defect would come back in a fresh costume, I pictured a…

articles.author: Nayan Kyada
articles.description:
Next.js API routes vs route handlers is one of those migrations that looks trivial in the docs but bites you on caching semantics and runtime defaults. Both surface HTTP endpoints inside a Next.js project, but they sit in fundamentally different mental models — one is a Node.js request/response wrapper, the other is built on the Web Fetch API and plays by App Router rules.
Pages Router API routes live at pages/api/**/*.ts. They receive a NextApiRequest (a thin wrapper over Node's IncomingMessage) and a NextApiResponse. The runtime is always Node.js. They are never statically analysed for caching by the framework — every request hits your serverless function.
App Router route handlers live at app/**/route.ts. They receive a standard Request and return a standard Response. Because they are W…
articles.title: Next.js API routes vs route handlers: when to use each

articles.description:
Every deprecated-runtime migration produces the same shape of pain: you bump one version number, redeploy, and get hit with errors that look unrelated to each other but are all downstream of the same jump. The errors aren't random — for a given upgrade path, they show up in a fairly predictable order.
This is a map, not a new deep dive. Each line below is a real, verbatim error with its own fix already written up — this just sequences them by which upgrade produces them, so you know what's coming before you hit it instead of debugging one surprise at a time.
You're doing this because AWS blocks python3.9 creates/updates Feb 1 / Mar 3 2027 (and earlier versions are already blocked). Python 3.12 removed a batch of stdlib modules in one release (PEP 632/594), so this path front-loads the most…
articles.title: "The AWS runtime-upgrade error map: which errors you'll hit, in what order, for each migration path"

I have a small static site on GitHub Pages. It is served from a project subpath:

Twelve times over about two weeks, I pinged IndexNow to get the pages crawled. Every single
api.indexnow.org  ->  202
bing.com/indexnow ->  202
yandex.com/indexnow -> 202

Twelve rounds later, site:shantj.github.io/sproutguard returned zero results on Bing. Not
IndexNow authenticates you by fetching a key file from your host. Unless you say otherwise,
https://<host>/<key>.txt

Note what is missing: the subpath. My key file is at /sproutguard/<key>.txt, because that
project site can put a file. The domain root belongs to my
https://shantj.github.io/<key>.txt   -> 404
https://shantj.github.io/            -> 404

So the verification fetch 404s, and the submission is rejected…

Marisol ran a small bakery — six tables, a case of morning pastries, a back room that smelled permanently of yeast and cinnamon. articles.author: mu mu
articles.description:
Have you ever opened social media, scrolled for 30 minutes, and closed it feeling even more drained than before?
Between AI-generated slop, rage-baiting algorithms, and endless ads, the internet often feels less like a space for connection and more like a loud, neon-lit casino.
A few weeks ago, after feeling overwhelmed by digital noise, I decided to code a small, quiet, dark-themed Q&A corner for myself and fellow web users who miss the simpler web.
It's called Ask A Monk:
https://askamonk.online


🧘 What makes it different?
Inspired by the quiet atmosphere of a monastery, I built Ask A Monk around three core principles:
Zero AI & Zero Algorithms: Every question and response comes from a real human being. There are no recommendation engines pushing controversial content to keep you hooked.
Complete Anonymity: No accounts, no sign-ups, and no social pressure for likes or upvotes.
Distraction-Free UX: A minimalist dark UI with warm typography that is gentle on your eyes.
🛠️ The Tech & Philosophy
I wanted to build something that feels fast, light, and completely free of modern bloatware. The interface focuses strictly on readable content and seamless navigation.
Whether you're looking for perspective on a personal dilemma or simply want to draw a quiet daily thought, it's a space meant for slowing down.
Feel free to stop by, draw a quote, or leave a question:
Visit Ask A Monk]
I'd genuinely love to hear your thoughts on the UI, UX, or the overall concept. How do you escape the noise on the modern web?
articles.title: Why I Built a Zero-AI, Zero-Algorithm Q&A Space for Distraction-Free Thoughts
